prompt:
You are a careful equity research analyst. Assess the competitive advantages (economic moat) and pricing power of the publicly listed company "AB" (ticker AB), and list its competitors. Use the most recent information you know. Never invent figures: use null when unsure. Be specific (products, numbers, years).

Reply with ONLY one JSON object, no other text, in exactly this shape:
{
 "name": "official company name", "ticker": "AB", "industry": "industry in a few words",
 "markets": ["the main product markets it competes in"],
 "mission": {"statement": "the company's own official mission statement, word for word as it publishes it; null if you are not sure of the exact wording (never paraphrase here)",
             "source": "where it is published, e.g. company website or 2025 annual report, or null",
             "plain": "what the mission means, in one short simple sentence"},
 "about": {"plain": "3-4 short sentences explaining what the company does, in simple everyday words a 12-year-old would understand; no jargon",
           "customers": "who buys from it, in one simple sentence",
           "everyday": "one sentence linking it to something ordinary people know or use, or null",
           "money": [ {"part": "business line in simple words", "share": decimal share of sales or null, "plain": "what it sells there, in a few simple words", "tag": "main|new|moonshot"} ]  (its main ways of making money, largest first, up to 6; also include any new business line or one with explosive, moonshot potential even if its sales are still small. tag: "main" = an established line that brings in a large part of sales; "new" = launched or entered in roughly the last 3 years; "moonshot" = could grow many times over or reshape the company, e.g. a new technology or market, even if unproven. Give each line one tag, the one that fits best)},
 "summary": "2-3 plain-English sentences on whether and why it has a competitive advantage",
 "pricingPower": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "specific evidence, e.g. price rises and what happened to volumes"},
 "moats": [ {"source": one of ["Brand and intangible assets","Switching costs","Network effects","Cost advantage and scale","Efficient scale","Counter-positioning","Process power (hard-to-copy know-how)","Cornered resource (exclusive asset or talent)"], "strength": "strong|moderate|weak|none", "evidence": "one or two specific sentences"} ]  (all 8 sources, in that order),
 "customers": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "customer satisfaction and loyalty: retention, NPS, reviews, repeat purchase"},
 "talent": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "ability to attract and keep top talent: employer rankings, reputation, pay"},
 "product": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "is the product best in class? independent benchmarks, awards, ecosystem"},
 "competitors": [ {"name": "company name", "ticker": "main listing ticker (exchange suffix if not US, e.g. 005930.KS) or null if private",
                   "usTicker": "ticker of its US listing or ADR that files reports with the SEC, or null", "overlap": "high|medium|low",
                   "note": "where they compete"} ]  (every significant competitor, most direct first, up to 15; include major private ones with ticker null),
 "estimates": [ {"name": "company name", "fy": "FY2025", "currency": "USD", "revenueUSDm": number, "revenueGrowth3y": decimal, "grossMargin": decimal, "operatingMargin": decimal, "netMargin": decimal} ]
   (approximate latest fiscal-year figures for the company itself and for every listed competitor; decimals, e.g. 0.42; null if unknown),
 "marketShare": [ {"market": "market name", "measure": "revenue|units|shipments|...", "latestYear": "2025", "earlierYear": "2020",
                   "rows": [ {"name": "company name", "latest": decimal or null, "earlier": decimal or null} ] } ]  (up to 3 of its main markets, the company and its main rivals),
 "threats": ["specific things that could weaken its advantage"],
 "ceo": {"name": "current CEO", "founder": true or false, "since": "YYYY", "background": "e.g. electrical engineer, Stanford MBA"},
 "checklist": { "<id>": {"verdict": "yes|partly|no|unknown", "evidence": "one specific sentence with names, numbers or examples"} }  for EVERY id below:
   "c1": Rule Breaker #1: is it the leader of an important industry that is still emerging and growing fast?
   "c2": Rule Breaker #2: why do customers choose it over rivals (brand, better value, innovation, culture, leadership), and is that advantage hard to copy and likely to last many years?
   "c3": Rule Breaker #5: do ordinary people recognise the name, is it the default leader in its field (like Google, Amazon, NVIDIA, Tesla, Intuitive Surgical, Netflix), and would customers recommend its product?
   "c4": Does it have an inspiring mission it keeps emphasising, with management driven by purpose rather than money? If it spends 10 years doing this, would it matter?
   "c6": What is the general public consensus about the company and its products or services? When people hear the name, what are the first few descriptive words that come to mind? Start the evidence with those words in quotes (e.g. “innovative, premium, reliable”), then say whether that impression is mostly positive.
   "c7": Is its total addressable market large and growing, riding a secular trend (like CRWD, NVDA, TSLA, AMZN)?
   "c8": Does it have room to expand into big new markets: in its name, its technology or its vision?
   "m1": Is the CEO a visionary with a clear picture of the future?
   "m2": Is the CEO a founder (or acting like one): long-term thinking, working extraordinarily hard, pouring heart and soul into building something that outlives them?
   "m4": Does the CEO lead by serving employees and customers?
   "m5": Has the CEO deliberately built a strong, distinctive culture that keeps inventing new products and technologies?
   "m6": Is the CEO deeply hands-on with the product and technology, ideally with an engineering background?
   "m7": Is the CEO a person of great character who cares about something bigger than profit? For successor CEOs: is stewardship aimed at the benefit of humanity?
   "m7b": Has the CEO been invited to give a commencement speech at a top university (Stanford, Harvard, MIT, etc.)? Name it.
   "m8b": Does the CEO have a distinctive, memorable personality (like Elon Musk, Alex Karp, Larry Page)?
   "m9": Has the CEO a strong record of execution and results?
   "m10": Is the CEO and company known for frugality (like Bezos's door desk)?
   "c10": Do its products solve problems for people all over the world, greatly improving the lives of a very large number of people (like NFLX, GOOG, ISRG)?
   "p2": Is what it builds extremely hard to do, and important to the world?
   "f1": Has revenue grown in almost every one of the last five years?
   "f2": Have gross and operating margins risen over the last five years?
   "f3": Is debt low compared with cash and cash flow, with positive shareholders' equity?
   "f4": Have operating income and operating cash flow risen over the last five years?
   "v1": Is its main product clearly the best in its field, with a practical reason an ordinary person can understand for choosing it over every alternative (like NVIDIA over AMD)?
   "v2": Is it widely seen as one of the best companies to work for (culture, mission, reputation, employer rankings)? Cite rankings.
   "c5": Do its products make the world better? If it disappeared overnight, who would notice and miss it, and why?
 "asOf": "YYYY-MM of the newest information you used"
}

result.name: AllianceBernstein Holding L.P.
result.industry: Asset management and private wealth management
markets: Private markets and alternatives (private credit, real estate debt)

mission.source: AllianceBernstein website, Purpose and Values page
mission.plain: Use deep research to find investments that help clients reach their goals.

about.plain: AllianceBernstein invests money for other people. Pension funds, insurance companies, families and everyday savers give it money, and its experts choose stocks, bonds and private loans to grow it. It charges a small yearly fee based on how much money it looks after. Its Bernstein Private Wealth arm helps wealthy families plan and manage their savings.
about.customers: Pension funds, insurers (including its parent Equitable), fund buyers through financial advisers, and wealthy families.
about.everyday: If you or your employer's retirement plan owns an AB mutual fund or ETF, AB is the company picking the investments.

money.plain: yearly fees on money it manages
fees for selling and servicing its retail funds
bonus fees when funds beat targets
private credit and real-estate loans for insurers and pensions

result.summary: AllianceBernstein has a modest competitive advantage: a respected research culture, a sticky private-wealth business and a captive client in majority owner Equitable. But it is a mid-sized active manager in an industry where scale and low-cost passive products win, and retail money can leave easily, so its moat is narrow.

pricingPower.evidence: Industry fees keep falling as money shifts to passive; AB's adjusted net revenues were flat in 2025 ($3.52B vs $3.53B) even though average AUM rose 7.5% to $826.0B, implying a lower average fee rate.

moats.evidence: The AB and Bernstein names are well known among institutions, advisers and wealthy families; Bernstein Private Wealth ended 2025 with $156.3B of AUM, though the brand means little to ordinary consumers.
Private-wealth clients and institutional mandates (pensions, insurers such as parent Equitable) are sticky, but retail fund money moves easily: retail had $9.1B of net outflows in 2025.
Asset management has no meaningful network effect; one client's use does not make the product better for another.
With $905.5B of AUM (June 2026) AB has scale and a 33.0% adjusted operating margin, but it is far smaller than BlackRock (~$14T) or Vanguard, which win on low-cost passive products.
The industry has thousands of competitors and low barriers in most product areas.
AB is a traditional active manager facing the shift to passive; its active ETF and private-markets push follows peers rather than undercutting them.
Decades of fundamental research and strong municipal-bond, fixed-income and private-credit franchises (e.g. commercial mortgage loans) are hard to rebuild quickly.
Majority owner Equitable (about 68.1% economic interest at June 30, 2026) gives AB a captive general-account client for private-credit and fixed-income mandates.

customers.evidence: Private Wealth had $2.4B of net inflows in 2025 and institutional clients are long-term, but total net outflows were $11.3B in 2025, mainly $9.1B from retail; Q2 2026 returned to $0.8B of net inflows.

talent.evidence: As a large research-driven manager it attracts finance professionals, but it does not appear prominently in broad best-employer rankings; it moved its headquarters from New York to Nashville.

product.evidence: AB is known for fixed income, municipal bonds and private credit, but performance varies by strategy and it is not the clear best-in-class provider across its range.

Retail outflows during periods of weak relative performance ($9.1B retail net outflows in 2025)
Dependence on Equitable as majority owner and large client, with the Equitable-Corebridge merger possibly changing priorities
Competition from Blackstone, Apollo and others in private credit
CEO transition: Seth Bernstein retires March 31, 2027 and Onur Erzan takes over April 1, 2027

ceo.name: Seth P. Bernstein (Onur Erzan to succeed him April 1, 2027)
ceo.background: Long-time J.P. Morgan asset-management executive; successor Onur Erzan is a former McKinsey senior partner with a Columbia MBA

c1.evidence: Asset management is a large, mature industry, and AB with $905.5B AUM (June 2026) is a mid-sized player far behind BlackRock (~$14T).

c2.evidence: Clients choose AB for its research-driven fixed income, municipal-bond and private-credit expertise and Bernstein's wealth advice, but these advantages can be matched by large rivals.

c3.evidence: Ordinary people rarely recognise AllianceBernstein; BlackRock, Vanguard and Fidelity are the default names in investing.

c4.evidence: Its purpose, 'Pursue Insight That Unlocks Opportunity', is a client-focused slogan rather than an inspiring world-changing mission.

c6.evidence: “institutional, research-driven, traditional” — a mostly positive but low-profile impression, known mainly to finance professionals and wealthy clients.

c7.evidence: Global investable assets keep growing and private markets are expanding, but active management's share is shrinking as money moves to passive.

c8.evidence: AB is expanding into private markets, active ETFs and India (AB India), but these are extensions of asset management rather than big new industries.

m1.evidence: Seth Bernstein repositioned the firm toward private markets and wealth and moved its headquarters to Nashville, but he is a disciplined manager rather than a visionary.

m2.evidence: Neither Seth Bernstein nor successor Onur Erzan is a founder; AB is majority-owned by Equitable.

m4.evidence: There is little public evidence either way about a servant-leadership style.

m5.evidence: AB promotes values such as 'Invest in One Another' and 'Strive for Distinctive Knowledge', but it is not known for inventing new products and technologies.

m6.evidence: Bernstein is a finance executive, not an engineer; investment products are run by portfolio teams.

m7.evidence: No notable controversies, but no strong public evidence of a mission beyond running the firm well.

m7b.evidence: No record found of Seth Bernstein giving a commencement speech at a top university.

m8b.evidence: He keeps a low public profile and is not a widely known personality.

m9.evidence: Under Bernstein, AUM nearly doubled to more than $919B by August 31, 2026 and adjusted operating margin rose from 30.1% (2020) to 33.7% (2025).

m10.evidence: Moving headquarters from New York to lower-cost Nashville was a deliberate cost-saving move.

c10.evidence: Its funds help millions of savers and pension members grow retirement money, but the service is easily replaced by rivals.

p2.evidence: Managing money well is skilled work, but many firms do it and it is not uniquely hard or world-changing.

f2.evidence: Adjusted operating margin rose from 30.1% (2020) to 33.7% (2025), but GAAP operating margin fell from 24.6% to 23.0%.

f3.evidence: At June 30, 2026 it had $896.5M cash vs $580.0M of borrowings, $950.1M of operating cash flow in six months, and $4.80B of partners' capital.

f4.evidence: GAAP operating income rose from $907M (2020) to $1,050M (2025), but dipped in 2022-2023 ($815M, $818M) and fell 6.5% in 2025.

v1.evidence: There is no clear reason an ordinary investor would pick AB funds over every alternative, such as cheaper index funds.

v2.evidence: AB is not commonly cited in major best-places-to-work rankings; no rankings verified.

c5.evidence: Clients would move to other managers fairly easily; its disappearance would mostly be noticed by its own clients and employees.
